Russia’s overnight drone barrage ignites fires across Ukrainian cities Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 27/08/2026 - 15:55 GMT+2 Russian strikes hit Ukraine’s Sumy and Odesa regions overnight on 27 August. At least one person was killed and seven injured, according to regional authorities. … More In Sumy, strikes hit a residential area, sparking fires that damaged homes and commercial buildings. Emergency crews were deployed to three locations as residents surveyed the damage. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT In Odesa, firefighters tackled several fires after what regional officials described as a large-scale attack lasting more than seven hours. A 16-storey residential building was among the structures damaged, along with a private house, garage, educational facilities, vehicles and a grain elevator. Ukraine’s Air Force said its defences had shot down or suppressed 233 Russian targets during the overnight barrage, including 258 attack drones, two Oniks anti-ship missiles and several Iskander-M and KN-23 ballistic missiles. The force said around a third of the drones were jet-powered, while others included Shahed-type, Gerbera and Banderol systems, as well as decoys. The attacks also caused damage in the Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Poltava and Zaporizhzhia regions. In Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said four people were injured, with two taken to hospital, after falling drone debris and fires hit several districts. A separate daytime strike on 27 August hit an Epicentr shopping centre in Kharkiv’s Osnovyanskyi district. Regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said a Russian Geran-4 Seeker drone killed one man and injured at least four others. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said emergency teams remained at work across the affected areas. Russian defence officials, meanwhile, said the barrage had targeted military-industrial sites, oil refineries, logistics hubs and port infrastructure. Illustration: equal-earth.com Japan Japan seeks change to new UN world map over Russia 'misconception' The new ‘true-scale’ map shrinks Europe and North America while enlarging Africa – and depicts the disputed Kuril islands as ruled by Moscow Agence France-Presse in Tokyo Thu 10 Sep 2026 08.55 EDT Last modified on Thu 10 Sep 2026 09.08 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Japan has asked for the revision of a new world map adopted by the UN because it said it made the disputed Kuril islands appear to belong to Russia . The UN general assembly voted on Friday to adopt the new map, which makes the African continent larger while also shrinking North America and Europe , drawing condemnation from the US. UN votes to adopt new world map that shows Africa’s true scale Read more Japan was among the 164 UN members that supported the resolution, but has now taken issue with it because it shows the Kurils, known in Japan as the Northern Territories, in the same colour as Russia. Japanese government spokesperson Minoru Kihara on Thursday said the new map – known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection – “contained a depiction contradicting the Japanese government’s position”. “We lodged a protest with the map site’s operator through our diplomatic channel to demand the correction of this depiction,” Kihara told reporters. He declined to say when the issue was brought to government’s attention but said Japan “needs to prevent misconceptions of our territories and geographical names from spreading”. The disputed islands were seized in 1945 by the former Soviet Union, which then expelled the Japanese population. View image in fullscreen The disputed Kuril islands, top right. Photograph: equal-earth.com Relations between Japan and Russia soured significantly last month, when Russian president, Vladimir Putin, made a surprise visit to the disputed islands for the first time. Japan swiftly summoned Moscow’s ambassador, with the prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, saying Putin’s visit “offends the sentiments of the Japanese people”, adding that it was “absolutely unacceptable”. She said the islands were “an inherent part of Japan’s territory, both historically and under international law”. Moscow quickly hit back, saying it “categorically” rejects such statements, “which we consider politically inappropriate, insulting and, of course, legally unfounded”. The UN said the new map aimed to present “a more accurate representation” of continental landmasses than was portrayed by more traditional Mercator projections. https://www.dw.com/en/why-indian-nationa.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PsHR Prefer DW on Google Modi raised Russian recruitment of Indians when they met in Moscow in July 2024 [FILE] Image: Alexander Zemlianichenko/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Gurpreet Singh Randhawa, a 40-year-old from Jalandhar in India's northern Punjab state, said he traveled to Russia for work after responding to a Facebook advertisement for a driving job at a garment factory. But instead of finding work as a driver, he was sent to fight in Ukraine for the Russian armed forces . After escaping from his unit, he surrendered to Ukrainian forces in November. He is now being held as a prisoner of war. In an interview with Ukrainian YouTuber Volodymyr Zolkin, Randhawa described how, after arriving in Russia, he was taken to a military facility, made to sign a contract and sent for training. He said they confiscated his passport and phone. His account has not been independently verified. Randhawa's story is a familiar one in India . He is the second Indian national known to have escaped the Russian military. Sahil Majothi, a 23-year-old from Gujarat, surrendered to Ukrainian forces in October 2025. He had joined the Russian military while serving a prison sentence in Russia, reportedly believing that military service would help him secure his release. Ukraine war: Plight of Indians trapped in Russian army To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video India's efforts to bring recruits home The cases underline how little has changed since Prime Minister Narendra Modi raised the issue with Russian President Vladimir Putin during his visit to Moscow in July 2024 . At the time, Putin assured him that Indians who were misled into joining the Russian army would be discharged. But the recruitment of Indians has continued. In an October filing before the Supreme Court, India's Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said approximately 267 Indians have joined the Russian armed forces since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine . Of these, 139 were discharged and 51 were killed. The whereabouts of the 77 others were unknown. Russian authorities have confirmed that seven of them are missing. The problem extends beyond Indians who travel to Russia seeking civilian employment, only to find themselves exposed to recruitment networks and the dangers of a war zone. The MEA has also highlighted cases of Indians knowingly enlisting in the Russian military for the supposed financial benefits on offer, believing they could later secure release through government intervention. Some had also approached Indian authorities to renounce their citizenship and obtain Russian passports. "This is a dangerous path and is strongly discouraged by the government," the ministry said. Lured into war: Russia's foreign fighters in Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Duped or desperate? Former diplomat Anil Trigunayat said the growing movement of Indian workers to Russia presents both economic opportunities and new challenges for their protection. "Inadequate oversight of recruitment networks could leave vulnerable workers exposed to exploitation," Trigunayat told DW. He said Indian workers were often burdened by substantial recruitment fees and continued deductions from their salaries by intermediaries. "Some of them had paid between 300,000 to 500,000 Indian rupees [$5,400 /€4,900] to Indian recruitment agents, and even while working in Russia, more than 30% of their agreed monthly salary was taken away by local and foreign agents," Trigunayat said. The former diplomat added that some Indians who had overstayed their visas in Russia were particularly vulnerable. Military service was allegedly offered to earn substantial wages and regularize their immigration status. Mohammad Sufiyan, from Hyderabad in the southern state of Telangana, said he was lured to Russia under false pretences and forced into active combat in Ukraine. He had traveled abroad in search of employment and a better livelihood, but ended up in a war zone. He has since returned home to India . "Many people are duped. Some decide it is better to seek citizenship than come back to India. It's a tough life, and people will go to any lengths to get some sort of employment," Sufiyan told DW. Sufiyan's experience points to the economic desperation that makes such offers attractive, even when they carry the risk of being caught up in a war. Rajan Kumar, a professor at the Center for Russian and Central Asian Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University's School of International Studies, said some Indians who traveled to Russia for work could find themselves caught up in the fighting without having joined the military. "Some of them, they don't join the army, but they end up in the army region. They're caught in the crossfire," Kumar told DW. He said India was negotiating with Moscow to secure the return of its citizens caught up in such situations. "Russia is very cooperative so far," he said. India's special relationship with Russia explained To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Moscow prioritizes military aims over strategic diplomacy India has been pressing Russia to take action, but the issue persists. The recruitment efforts reflect Russia's need for more manpower for its nearly five-year war in Ukraine , and the limited influence New Delhi can exert over Moscow, despite the close political relationship between the two countries. Mohsin Raza Khan, a professor at the Jindal School of International Affairs, told DW that Putin 's need to sustain the war effort was taking precedence over the concerns of a strategic partner. He points out that the Russian president was reluctant to impose another mobilization on his own population for fear of domestic unrest. "In these circumstances, sustaining the war effort appears to take precedence over concerns raised by India. Neither Modi nor New Delhi has sufficient leverage to change that," said Khan. Khan also said the willingness of some Indians to enlist, and even consider giving up their citizenship, is down to the lack of decent employment opportunities at home. "For young, educated men without contacts or connections, the chances of respectable employment are so low that the risks of a high casualty war are preferable," he said.
